Set 1.primary_i_can: I can identify the reference frame used in a motion description.
Set 1.student_text: A motion description says, “The backpack remains beside Leo on the seat while trees move backward past the window.” Identify the reference frame used when the backpack is described as remaining beside Leo, and cite the cue.
Set 1.student_html:
A motion description says, “The backpack remains beside Leo on the seat while trees move backward past the window.” Identify the reference frame used when the backpack is described as remaining beside Leo, and cite the cue.

  1. no reference frame is needed
  2. the vehicle/passenger frame
  3. the trees outside
  4. the backpack itself only
choices: no reference frame is needed
the vehicle/passenger frame
the trees outside
the backpack itself only
Set 1.answer: The vehicle/passenger frame; the backpack stays at a fixed position relative to the passenger/seat.
Set 1.solution_text: A reference frame is the object or coordinate system used to judge position and motion. “Beside the passenger on the seat” fixes the backpack relative to the vehicle.

Set 1.primary_i_can: I can compare motion from two different points of view and explain why everyday motion is usually described relative to Earth’s surface.
Set 1.student_text: A passenger on a bus says a phone on the seat is at rest. A person on the sidewalk says the phone is moving east with the bus. Compare the two descriptions and explain why using Earth’s surface is convenient for ordinary travel descriptions.
Set 1.student_html: A passenger on a bus says a phone on the seat is at rest. A person on the sidewalk says the phone is moving east with the bus. Compare the two descriptions and explain why using Earth’s surface is convenient for ordinary travel descriptions.
Set 1.answer: Both descriptions can be correct because they use different reference frames. The phone is at rest in the bus frame and moving in the Earth/sidewalk frame. Earth’s surface is a convenient shared everyday frame.
Set 1.solution_text: Motion is relative; Earth is a convenient shared everyday frame.

Set 1.primary_i_can: I can compare motion from two different points of view and explain why everyday motion is usually described relative to Earth’s surface.
Set 1.student_text: A cyclist reports 6 m/s east relative to the road while a rider beside the cyclist says the cyclist is nearly at rest relative to the moving group. Compare the descriptions and identify why Earth’s surface is often the convenient everyday frame.
Set 1.student_html: A cyclist reports 6 m/s east relative to the road while a rider beside the cyclist says the cyclist is nearly at rest relative to the moving group. Compare the descriptions and identify why Earth’s surface is often the convenient everyday frame.
Set 1.answer: Both descriptions can be valid because velocity is frame-dependent; Earth’s surface gives a stable shared reference for ordinary locations and travel.
Set 1.solution_text: Reference frames change measured motion, not the object itself.

Set 1.primary_i_can: I can explain why an object can be moving relative to one reference frame but not another.
Set 1.student_text: Mina walks toward the front of a train moving east at 12 m/s. Mina walks at 2 m/s relative to the train. Explain how Mina can be moving relative to the ground while also being described using a different motion relative to the train.
Set 1.student_html:
Mina walks toward the front of a train moving east at 12 m/s. Mina walks at 2 m/s relative to the train. Explain how Mina can be moving relative to the ground while also being described using a different motion relative to the train.

  1. Mina must have the same velocity in every reference frame.
  2. Mina is at rest relative to the ground because the train is the only valid frame.
  3. Reference frames change the object’s mass, which changes its motion.
  4. Relative to the train, Mina moves east at 2 m/s; relative to the ground, Mina moves east at 14 m/s. Motion depends on the chosen reference frame.
choices: Mina must have the same velocity in every reference frame.
Mina is at rest relative to the ground because the train is the only valid frame.
Reference frames change the object’s mass, which changes its motion.
Relative to the train, Mina moves east at 2 m/s; relative to the ground, Mina moves east at 14 m/s. Motion depends on the chosen reference frame.
Set 1.answer: Relative to the train, Mina moves east at 2 m/s; relative to the ground, Mina moves east at 14 m/s. Motion depends on the chosen reference frame.
Set 1.solution_text: Use one reference frame at a time. The train-frame motion is the walking speed; the ground-frame motion combines train and walking motion because both are east.

Set 1.solution_text: Velocity includes magnitude and direction, so a direction change changes velocity.

Set 1.primary_i_can: I can distinguish instantaneous speed from average speed.
Set 1.student_text: On a bike path, a rider’s speedometer reads 14 m/s at one instant. The rider’s average speed over the entire trip is 7 m/s. Explain what each value describes.
Set 1.student_html:
On a bike path, a rider’s speedometer reads 14 m/s at one instant. The rider’s average speed over the entire trip is 7 m/s. Explain what each value describes.

  1. The larger value is average and the smaller value is instantaneous by definition.
  2. 14 m/s is instantaneous speed at that moment; 7 m/s is total distance divided by total trip time.
  3. Both values are instantaneous because both use m/s.
  4. Both values are average because every speed is averaged over time.
choices: The larger value is average and the smaller value is instantaneous by definition.
14 m/s is instantaneous speed at that moment; 7 m/s is total distance divided by total trip time.
Both values are instantaneous because both use m/s.
Both values are average because every speed is averaged over time.
Set 1.answer: 14 m/s is instantaneous speed at that moment; 7 m/s is total distance divided by total trip time.
Set 1.solution_text: Instantaneous speed describes one moment. Average speed combines the whole interval: total distance divided by total elapsed time.

Extra Practice.primary_i_can: I can compare velocity vectors to determine whether an object’s velocity is changing.
Extra Practice.student_text: Vector A is 4 cm long and points east. Vector B is 4 cm long and points north. Determine whether the object’s velocity changed and explain what feature of the vectors supports your answer.
Extra Practice.student_html:
Vector A is 4 cm long and points east. Vector B is 4 cm long and points north. Determine whether the object’s velocity changed and explain what feature of the vectors supports your answer.

  1. Yes only if the arrow lengths also change.
  2. Yes. The speed magnitude can be the same, but the direction changes from east to north, so velocity changes.
  3. No; equal arrow lengths guarantee equal velocity.
  4. No; direction is not part of velocity.
Show your reasoning here.
choices: Yes only if the arrow lengths also change.
Yes. The speed magnitude can be the same, but the direction changes from east to north, so velocity changes.
No; equal arrow lengths guarantee equal velocity.
No; direction is not part of velocity.
Extra Practice.answer: Yes. The speed magnitude can be the same, but the direction changes from east to north, so velocity changes.
Extra Practice.solution_text: Velocity vectors are equal only when both magnitude and direction are equal. Changing direction changes velocity.
